body.text: The firings documented in detail involve the SR-71's CIA forerunner, the A-12. North Vietnam fired surface-to-air missiles at A-12s on three BLACK SHIELD missions. On 28 October 1967 one missile, launched too late, was never a threat. Two days later at least six were fired at Dennis Sullivan, flying Article 129 (60-6932) at Mach 3.1 and 84,000 ft; he saw three detonations behind him. A CIA memorandum of 6 November 1967 records a single hole "approximately the size" of one made by a .30-06 round, in a fillet just aft of the starboard landing gear, where a pellet had pierced the skin and a support for one of the fuel tanks. A third missile, on 4 January 1968, burst well over a mile away. The Blackbird family was hit once, by a fragment.

citations.detail: pp. 36 to 37; mission table pp. 50 to 51 (BX6734, Sullivan, 129)

body.text: For the SR-71 itself, single firings are recorded but never totalled. The Roadrunners timeline, citing Paul Crickmore's book Lockheed SR-71: The Secret Missions Exposed, dates the first confirmed SA-2 launch at an SR-71 to 26 July 1968, against 61-7974 flown by Tony Bevacqua and Jerry Crew, and says the aircraft's own cameras photographed the missile. The best documented case came on 26 August 1981. The next day the State Department said that North Korea had "fired a missile at a U.S. Air Force plane flying in South Korean and international air space" and called it "an act of lawlessness". The Department of State Bulletin's chronology names the aircraft as an SR-71 near the Demilitarized Zone and adds that it was not hit.

citations.detail: entry for 26 Jul 1968; source key SME (Crickmore)
p. 39 (Department statement, 27 Aug 1981) and p. 85 (chronology, 26 Aug)

body.text: The people who sent the aircraft did not treat it as untouchable. Asking Henry Kissinger in March 1973 to approve new flights over North Vietnam, the Director of Central Intelligence, James Schlesinger, called the SR-71 the only airborne platform that could cover the targets "with reasonable safety". The loss record, by contrast, is not in dispute. Lockheed built 32 SR-71s and 12 were lost, all in accidents; the 9th Reconnaissance Wing says none was lost to enemy fire. At least two came down on operational sorties. A CIA summary records that on 10 May 1970 a GIANT SCALE aircraft "crashed after one successful pass over denied territory", 25 km north-east of U-Tapao in Thailand, with both crew safe, and 61-7974 was lost off Luzon on 21 April 1989. Veterans' chronologies blame a centre-of-gravity problem and an engine explosion, not the enemy.

By the time the SR-71 retired, the escape from missiles had become part of its farewell. The White House news summary for 7 March 1990 records NBC's Fred Francis telling viewers on 6 March that no aircraft had "dodged more missiles than the Blackbird", in a report that also had it photographing targets inside the Soviet Union, work the Smithsonian says satellites had already taken over by the time the SR-71 entered service. No count was given then either.

differ.text: The counts disagree and none is tied to a published tally. Airman (10 July 2017) says 4,000; the 9th Reconnaissance Wing article on DVIDS (4 March 2020) says "over a recorded number of 1,000"; the Air & Space Forces Magazine entry says "more than 1,000"; the Roadrunners timeline attributes "over 1000" to Kelly Johnson on 31 August 1981; Charles Allen (2015) recalled about 800 over North Vietnam alone. Smaller details differ too: CIA's Archangel says the 1967 fragment penetrated the A-12's lower right wing and lodged near the fuel tank, while the 6 November 1967 memorandum places the hole in a fillet just aft of the starboard landing gear. The 10 May 1970 loss is put near Korat in the Roadrunners timeline and 25 km north-east of U-Tapao in the CIA summary.

title: New York to London in under two hours
dek: On 1 September 1974 an SR-71 crossed the Atlantic in 1 hour 54 minutes, and twelve days later a second crew raced the same aircraft home from London to Los Angeles.

body.text: On 30 August 1974 the Pentagon told newsreel editors that an Air Force SR-71 would try for a speed record between New York and London on 1 September, "as part of an overseas training mission". The crew would be Maj. James V. Sullivan, 37, the pilot, and Maj. Noel F. Widdifield, 33, his reconnaissance systems officer, both of the 9th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing at Beale Air Force Base, California, with a second crew standing by. The time to beat was 4 hours 46 minutes, set by a Royal Navy F-4K Phantom in 1969, and the release predicted the SR-71 would take nearly three hours off it. The aircraft was bound for the Farnborough International 74 air show in England.

The run began on the far side of the continent. The Air Force film of the flight shows the crew boarding at Beale before midnight on 31 August, then the aircraft slowing and descending off the coast of North Carolina to take fuel from a tanker before lining up on the timing gate over New York and accelerating beyond Mach 3 towards 80,000 ft. Guinness World Records, which still lists the flight, says it crossed the New York radar gate at about 80,000 ft and slowed to refuel once from a KC-135. After a great-circle crossing the aircraft passed a second gate near London, flew over Farnborough and landed there.

The time for the 3,461.53 statute miles (5,570.80 km) was 1 hour 54 minutes 56.4 seconds, an average of 1,806.96 mph (2,908.02 km/h), less than half the old record. The aircraft was 61-7972. That morning President Gerald Ford, at Camp David, spent four minutes on a conference line with Sullivan and Widdifield; his diary records that he called "to congratulate the crew".

61-7972 stayed on static display at Farnborough until 8 September, the first time an SR-71 had been shown in public outside the United States. The film's narrator names Kelly Johnson, the aircraft's designer, among those who met it, and the film shows the crews answering visitors' questions and signing fact sheets beside the aircraft.

For the journey home the aircraft was moved to RAF Mildenhall and handed to a second crew, Capt. Harold B. "Buck" Adams and Maj. William C. Machorek. Buz Carpenter's Blackbird timeline records a first attempt on 12 September that turned back with an oil warning light. On 13 September they crossed the London gate, slowed to refuel over Hudson Bay, and announced themselves over the Los Angeles gate with a sonic boom before turning north to land at Beale. The time was 3 hours 47 minutes 39 seconds for about 5,447 statute miles, close to 1,435.5 mph, and there was no earlier record to break.

On 19 September Ford received both crews in the Oval Office, with Senator Barry Goldwater, the Secretary of the Air Force, John L. McLucas, and the Chief of Staff, Gen. David C. Jones, and posed with them for the press. The White House notice issued that day rounded the times to "1 hour and 56 minutes" and "3 hours and 48 minutes", and said the SR-71 had passed 2,000 mph and 80,000 ft on both flights.

61-7972 flew on with the Air Force until 6 March 1990, when it set one more record on its last flight, Los Angeles to Washington, and was handed to the Smithsonian. It is on display in the Boeing Aviation Hangar of the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Virginia.

differ.text: The figures change with the source. For New York to London, Guinness, This Day in Aviation and Carpenter give 1 hour 54 minutes 56.4 seconds over 3,461.5 statute miles; the White House notice of 19 September rounds the time to 1 hour 56 minutes; the Air Force film's narrator gives "1 hour, 55 minutes, 32 seconds" for a "3,470 statute mile trip"; and a 2014 Beale AFB history piece pairs the film's 3,470 miles with the 1:54:56.4 time. For London to Los Angeles, Carpenter gives 5,447 miles at 1,435.59 mph, This Day in Aviation 5,446.87 miles at 1,435.49 mph, the film 5,463 statute miles and Hildebrant's timeline 5,645 miles; Carpenter, This Day in Aviation and the film agree on 3 hours 47 minutes 39 seconds. The White House notice dates the return 11 September, against 13 September in Carpenter and in the National Archives title of the Air Force's film of the arrival at Beale. On refuelling, the Pentagon's release planned "aerial refuelings" (plural), the film shows one off North Carolina before the New York gate, and Guinness says the aircraft slowed to refuel once. And where it first landed: the National Archives shot list has 61-7972 landing at Farnborough on 1 September, while Hildebrant's timeline says the first SR-71 to come to Britain landed at RAF Mildenhall.

title: NICE GIRL: the fly-off that settled nothing
dek: In the autumn of 1967 the CIA's A-12 and the Air Force's SR-71 flew the same tracks an hour apart to decide which to keep; the cameras gave one answer and the budget another.

body.text: The CIA's A-12 was condemned before it flew a single mission. On 12 December 1966 Cyrus Vance, Charles Schultze and Donald Hornig outvoted Richard Helms on how to cut the cost of two Mach 3 reconnaissance fleets, and on 28 December President Johnson ordered the CIA program ended by 1 January 1968, leaving the work to the Air Force's SR-71. Then the A-12s went to war over North Vietnam from May 1967, the SR-71 was not ready, and senior officials began to have doubts.

On paper the two aircraft were close. The National Reconnaissance Office told the intelligence community in September 1967 that there was little difference in range, that the lighter A-12 flew 2,000 to 5,000 feet higher at the same Mach number, and that the SR-71 carried photographic, radar, infrared and electronic sensors where the A-12 carried one main package. For the hunt for missiles in North Vietnam, it judged both adequate. Heat limits on its wing-tank sealant then held the SR-71 to Mach 3.0.

So they were made to race. A meeting on 16 October gave the exercise its name, NICE GIRL, and a cable the next day set the rules: tracks and camera legs "identical within limits of respective navigation systems", each aircraft launching from its own base, Mach 3.1 on the sensor legs, no more than an hour between the two, and a go only if cloud covered half the legs or less. "For security purposes," it added, "both aircraft are to be considered SR-71's." Between 20 October and 3 November they flew three routes along the Mississippi River.

citations.detail: cable of 17 October 1967, paras. A-B and pp. 3-6, 10

body.text: Photo-interpreters from NPIC and the Defense Intelligence Agency picked the targets: on the first route, 86 within reach of the A-12's Type I camera and 21 that only an SR-71 sensor could cover. The verdict, in Archangel's words, was "inconclusive". The A-12's camera had a wider swath and better resolution; the SR-71 gathered kinds of intelligence the A-12 could not, though not yet of very good quality, and some of its sensors would have to come out to make room for jammers.

The CIA argued harder than that. Before a review meeting on 20 December, its science chief, Carl Duckett, wrote to Helms that the SR-71's technical camera "clearly does not even come close to performing up to specifications", and that of two cameras of similar resolution the A-12's covered "almost three times as much area per flight". Matching it, he reckoned, would take six or more SR-71s at Kadena instead of three A-12s.

The A-12 won time, not the argument. On 29 December Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Nitze extended its operations through 30 June 1968 with five aircraft, while the SR-71 was readied for North Vietnam "as rapidly as ECM implementation and other program considerations will permit". SR-71s arrived at Kadena in March and flew their first mission over North Vietnam on 21 March. In April Helms pointed to 28 overflights, an "unusually high reliability" and "valuable intelligence", and asked to keep the fleet under CIA management.

It made no difference. Defense Secretary Clark Clifford reaffirmed the termination on 16 May 1968, and Johnson confirmed it at his weekly lunch on 21 May. Four days later the NRO ordered every A-12 into storage and that the contractors be told the program was ending; the last went into storage at Palmdale, California, on 21 June. Kelly Johnson wrote in his project log that it was "a bleak end for a program that has been overall as successful as this."

differ.text: Archangel says the aircraft flew "three identical routes"; the planning cables of 17 and 31 October name two routes, planned two missions for each aircraft on 20 and 25 October with 27 October in reserve, and the released cables number the A-12 sorties NX7521 (flown 25 October) and NX7522. Archangel credits the A-12 with "higher resolution"; Duckett called the two cameras of "approximately similar resolution". McIninch and Archangel's timeline date Johnson's original decision to 28 December 1966; the CIA's June 1968 submission to the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board says 29 December.

title: Rescued by Viggens
dek: When an engine exploded at Mach 3 over the Baltic in 1987, a crippled SR-71 found its escort in four Swedish fighter pilots, whose part stayed secret for thirty years.

body.text: In the 1980s the U.S. Air Force flew regular SR-71 reconnaissance missions over the international waters of the Baltic Sea, known as "Baltic Express" missions. Sweden watched them closely. Briefing guests at a ceremony in 2018, retired Swedish colonel Per-Olof Eldh said Swedish records count 322 such missions between 1977 and 1988, entering south of Copenhagen, running east at Mach 3 and returning south through the narrow international corridor between Öland and Gotland, where JA 37 Viggen pilots practised intercepts against them. On 29 June 1987 one SR-71 left RAF Mildenhall in England with two tasks, the Barents Sea first and then the Baltic.

Its crew were the pilot, Duane Noll, and the reconnaissance systems officer, Tom Veltri. Off the Baltic states, heading north at about 22,000 m and Mach 3, the right engine exploded. Veltri recalled that it went as he counted down to a turn point, and that the aircraft then fell about 40,000 ft in less than a minute. He set the emergency code on the transponder, and they turned south towards Gotland, levelling at about 25,000 ft and 380 knots. They knew, he said, that they were now an easy target. Försvarsmakten, the Swedish Armed Forces, has the aircraft down to 7,500 m within a minute or so and crossing into Swedish airspace level with Gotland.

Swedish air defence saw it at once. Eldh, then a squadron commander at F 13 at Norrköping, said his notes record a call from the sector operations centre at about 14:56 asking for every fighter available. The only ones near were two unarmed JA 37s of F 13 on an exercise near Västervik, flown by Roger Möller and Krister Sjöberg. Möller recalled being asked to identify "a certain interest" and guessing at once that it was an SR-71. Told it was already over Gotland, he went supersonic and found it in cloud at about 25,000 ft. The pair stayed with it for about five minutes, at times only 30 m away; Möller saw that it was flying on one engine and read the number 117964. Short of fuel, they turned for home as a second pair arrived.

That pair was the armed quick-reaction alert of F 6, normally based at Karlsborg but standing alert at Ängelholm on the west coast: Lars-Erik Blad and his wingman, Bo Ignell. Blad recalled scrambling in fog and drizzle so thick that he doubted they could land again. They reached the SR-71 about 70 km east of Bornholm, in international airspace. So as not to startle the crew, Blad flew a gentle pass along its right side, then turned a full circle to settle behind and above it, while Ignell held close on the right and photographed the crippled aircraft. It kept losing height. The Viggens stayed with it until it reached Danish airspace, by which time, Blad said, they were down to about 4,000 m and had seen no other aircraft.

Veltri said he first saw two fighters closing from the east, from the direction of the Soviet Union, and thought this could be the end until he made out Swedish markings. In 2018 he said that a MiG-25 came within a few miles soon after the Viggens joined, and that he later learned from the National Security Agency that Soviet fighters had orders to force the SR-71 down or shoot it down. He recalled that fog had closed Denmark, that F-15s from West Germany took over the escort, and that they landed at Nordholz with the auxiliary hydraulics gone, stopping in the overrun. Försvarsmakten confirms the landing at Nordholz.

The U.S. Air Force says the details stayed classified until 2017. Veltri said he had spent 31 years trying to find the Swedish pilots until a Saab representative he met at an Air Force Association event put him in touch, and that he then worked with the Air Staff to have them recognised. On 28 November 2018, at the U.S. ambassador's residence in Stockholm, Maj. Gen. John Williams of U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa presented the Air Medal, before Sweden's Supreme Commander, Air Force chief and defence minister. Blad, Möller and Sjöberg received theirs in person; Ignell could not attend. The citation credits them with shielding the SR-71 from any third-party aircraft and escorting it beyond Swedish territory. Noll, unable to travel, sent a recorded message: "because of you, there was no international incident."

differ.text: Accounts differ in detail. Height when the engine failed: about 22,000 m (Försvarsmakten), over 80,000 ft (Veltri) or 70,000 ft (Eldh). Place: the U.S. Air Force story has the Viggens intercepting "over Swedish airspace", the Air Medal citation says international waters, and Försvarsmakten puts the first meeting east of Öland after the SR-71 had crossed Gotland and the second in international airspace east of Bornholm. Units: the citation and the U.S. Embassy place all four pilots at F 13 Bråvalla, but Försvarsmakten and Blad put Blad and Ignell in the F 6 alert pair at Ängelholm. Landing: the citation as read at the ceremony names a NATO base in Denmark; the embassy says Germany, and Försvarsmakten and Veltri name Nordholz. Soviet fighters: only Veltri reports a MiG-25 and Soviet orders, from later intelligence he has not published; Blad told Försvarsmakten he saw no other aircraft. Försvarsmakten calls Veltri one of the pilots; he was the reconnaissance systems officer. Names are spelt Lars-Erik or Lars-Eric Blad, Möller or Moller, Sjöberg or Sjoberg. The serial 61-7964 rests on Möller's reading of "117964" as Försvarsmakten reports it; no U.S. source found names the aircraft.

title: The A-12 that went by road
dek: Too secret to fly and too big for any cargo plane, the first A-12 left Burbank in a crate 105 feet long on a February night in 1962, and nine weeks later it was in the air.

body.text: The first A-12, Article 121 (60-6924), was finished at Lockheed's Skunk Works in Burbank and spent January and February 1962 in final ground tests. It was badly late. The CIA had been promised a first aircraft at the end of May 1961, and trouble with titanium and with the J58 engine had pushed the date back again and again. On 1 February 1962 the CIA's Special Projects Branch still listed Aircraft 1 for delivery on 21 February and a first flight on 21 March.

Flying it to Nevada was never an option. The aircraft was too secret to fly to the test site, too large for a cargo aircraft, and the runway at Burbank was not adequate. Lockheed had done it once already, in November 1959, when it trucked a full-scale radar model from Burbank to the test area on a specially designed trailer. A survey of the route in June 1961 showed that a package 35 feet wide and 105 feet long could make the journey if road signs were taken down, trees trimmed and some roadsides levelled, and police and local officials were brought into the plan.

For the trip Article 121 was partly taken apart. The whole fuselage, without its wings, was crated, covered and loaded on a purpose-built trailer that cost about $100,000; the wings went separately, to be fitted at the site. On the night of 26 February 1962 the load left the Skunk Works, escorted by the California and Nevada highway patrols and CIA security officers. According to the CIA's 1992 history of the programme, it reached the Nevada base, known as Area 51, two days later.

The road was the most exposed part of a secret project. When Article 122 made the same journey in June 1962, a Greyhound bus coming the other way grazed its 35-foot-wide crate, and project managers paid for the damage at once so that no insurance claim or court case would ask why the load was so wide. In November 1962 the CIA's Office of Security kept a loose watch on another A-12 convoy, and afterwards the security branch reported that public guesses about the cargo still varied, "however, people are starting to count."

At the base, reassembly and the fitting of two interim Pratt & Whitney J75 engines began, and so did a new delay. When fuel first went into the tanks, the sealing compound came away from the metal; the CIA's 1992 history counts 68 leaks. The tanks were stripped and resealed, a slow job because the sealant needed four curing cycles at different temperatures, each lasting 30 to 54 hours.

On 25 April 1962 Lockheed test pilot Lou Schalk made the unannounced first hop that Lockheed custom called for. Wrongly connected controls set up what Kelly Johnson called "lateral oscillations which were horrible to see", and after less than two miles at about 20 feet Schalk put the aircraft down on the lakebed beyond the runway. The next day he flew for about 40 minutes with the landing gear down, and the A-12 shed titanium fillets from its chines; technicians spent four days finding and refitting them.

The official first flight followed on 30 April 1962, with Herbert Scoville, Richard Bissell and senior Air Force officers watching. Schalk flew for 59 minutes and climbed to 30,000 feet. The cable to headquarters began "FIRST FLIGHT GREAT SUCCESS" and quoted Johnson calling it the "SMOOTHEST FIRST FLIGHT IN HIS EXPERIENCE." On 4 May Article 121 went supersonic, reaching Mach 1.1 at 40,000 feet, and John McCone, the Director of Central Intelligence, telegraphed his congratulations to Johnson. The aircraft that had travelled to Nevada in a box went on to make 332 flights totalling 418.2 hours, and it is now on display at the Blackbird Airpark in Palmdale, California.

differ.text: Sources disagree on several dates. Arrival: the CIA histories have Article 121 leaving Burbank on 26 February 1962 (McIninch says only that it arrived according to plan; Pedlow and Welzenbach say two days later), and NASA historian Peter Merlin says the first airframe was delivered in February 1962, but the National Security Archive's 2013 briefing book says the first A-12 arrived at Area 51 in late December 1961. First flight: Robarge and Pedlow and Welzenbach give a short hop on 25 April and a 40-minute flight on 26 April, which Pedlow and Welzenbach also call the 'official' maiden flight before naming 30 April as the official first flight; McIninch and Kelly Johnson's 1981 paper give 26 April as the first flight and do not mention the hop; Archangel's own timeline lists 26 April. First supersonic flight: 4 May 1962 in the day-of cable, Archangel and McIninch, but 2 May in Pedlow and Welzenbach. The bus payment: 'nearly $5,000' (Archangel) or $4,890 (Pedlow and Welzenbach).

title: RS-71 or SR-71?
dek: The best-known story about the Blackbird's name says a president fumbled two letters; his own recording says otherwise.

verdict.text: Johnson did not garble the name. The official transcript and the White House recording have him say "SR-71" every time he names the aircraft, and a printed copy of the statement from August 1964 agrees. "RS-71" was a real name in Washington that summer: a senator used it on the Senate floor five days later, and a congressman was still using it in 1965. The claim that the President swapped the letters first appears, in the earliest dated source this project has found, in the CIA's Archangel of 2007, which gives no source for it. The Air Force's own account says the designation was changed to SR before the speech and that press material still carried RS-71. No draft of the statement or press handout reading RS-71 has yet been found to settle which account is right.

body.text: At half past three on the afternoon of Friday 24 July 1964, in the State Department Auditorium, Lyndon Johnson opened his twenty-third news conference with an aeroplane. He announced "a major new strategic manned aircraft system" for Strategic Air Command, built around "the new SR-71 aircraft", which would fly at more than three times the speed of sound and above 80,000 feet. The billion-dollar program, he said, had begun in February 1963. Then he turned to record farm exports.

The story told about that moment ever since is that the Air Force had called the aircraft the RS-71, for reconnaissance and strike, and that Johnson read the letters backwards. Rather than correct the President, the story goes, the Air Force kept his version and created a strategic reconnaissance category to fit it. The CIA's own history of the A-12, David Robarge's Archangel, tells it in just those terms: Johnson "mistakenly transposed the designator letters", and "Air Force officials let the error stand".

The record of the day does not bear this out. The official transcript has Johnson say "SR-71" every time he names the aircraft, and in the same statement he speaks of the RS-70, a different aircraft reviewed by the Joint Chiefs, with its letters in their proper order. The White House Communications Agency recording of the conference, now at the LBJ Library, has "SR-71" about 34 seconds in, again at 58 seconds and once more at 1 minute 39 seconds. A printed copy of the statement that the CIA filed on 3 August 1964 reads "SR-71" as well, and the next morning's New York Herald Tribune glossed the letters for its readers as "Strategic Reconnaissance".

Yet RS-71 was not invented later. On 29 July, five days after the announcement, Senator Gordon Allott of Colorado told the Senate that the President had announced a new plane "which I believe is now designated as the RS-71", and went on to object that a billion dollars for this "new RS-71 plane, formerly known as the A-11" had been hidden in the defence budget. The confusion lasted. In closed House Armed Services Committee hearings reported by Aviation Week in May 1965, the chairman asked about the "SR-71", the Air Force Chief of Staff, Gen. John P. McConnell, answered "YF-12", and Representative William H. Bates offered "RS-71".

Behind the secrecy the aircraft had already worn several names. Lockheed's two-seat development of the A-12 was the R-12, and Air Force officials were interested in a reconnaissance and strike variant, the RS-12, which, in NASA historian Peter Merlin's words, was "eventually re-designated SR-71". CIA memoranda called the Air Force aircraft the R-12 in December 1962 and still did so in August 1964, a month after the President had given it a public name. Archangel says the Air Force's first six were ordered as RS-71s.

The Air Force tells it differently. A 2014 history note from the 9th Reconnaissance Wing at Beale says that the Chief of Staff, Gen. Curtis LeMay, preferred SR for strategic reconnaissance, that the designation was changed before the speech, and that the media transcripts still carried RS-71, "thus creating the rumor that the president misread" it. That account fits the transcript and the recording, and it would explain why RS-71 lingered on Capitol Hill. But it cites no document, and it puts the announcement a day late, on 25 July.

Each part of the story can be dated. "SR-71" is in the President's own words on the day and in the transcript published from them. "RS-71" is on the Senate floor within the week. The claim that joins them, that the President swapped the letters, is the one that travelled, yet the earliest dated telling this project has found is the CIA's web edition of Archangel, posted in October 2007 without a source and repeated unchanged in the 2012 edition.

differ.text: Two official accounts disagree. The CIA's Archangel (web edition 2007; second edition 2012, p. 53) says Johnson transposed the letters and the Air Force let the error stand. The 9th Reconnaissance Wing's 2014 history note says Gen. Curtis LeMay had the designation changed to SR-71 before the speech and that media transcripts still read RS-71. Neither cites a document. The same Air Force note dates the announcement 25 July 1964; the transcript places the news conference at 3:30 p.m. on Friday 24 July 1964. Internal names also differ: CIA memoranda use R-12, Merlin traces R-12 and RS-12 to SR-71, and Archangel says the first contract was for six RS-71s.

title: Six missiles over Hanoi
dek: On 30 October 1967 North Vietnam fired a salvo of SA-2s at Dennis Sullivan's A-12; he flew on through them, and a sliver of metal came home lodged beside a fuel tank.

body.text: By the autumn of 1967 the CIA's A-12s had been flying BLACK SHIELD missions from Kadena, Okinawa, for five months, photographing North Vietnam for any sign of surface-to-surface missiles. They crossed it at Mach 3.1 to 3.2 and a little above 80,000 feet, and on the first fifteen missions nobody fired at them. That changed on 28 October, on the 16th mission, when a single SA-2 rose toward Dennis Sullivan in Article 131 (60-6937). It was launched too late, and the aircraft was already beyond its reach.

Two days later Sullivan was back over the North in Article 129 (60-6932) on mission BX6734, the 18th of the operation. He left Kadena at 0219 GMT on 30 October to make two photographic passes. On the first, radar tracked him and two missile sites made ready but did not fire. On the second, heading for Hanoi from the west at Mach 3.1 and 84,000 feet, his jammers began answering FAN SONG guidance radars from at least six sites at once, as battalions of two North Vietnamese missile regiments tried to engage him.

Sullivan raised his rear-view periscope. His report, quoted in the CIA's later analysis, described missiles "in a steep climb through the aircraft altitude of approximately 83,500 feet" that pushed over, levelled off and "guided toward the stern of the aircraft to detonation." He counted at least six contrails and three detonations, all behind him, and saw one missile climbing 100 to 200 yards off his right side, abeam the cockpit. Fourteen seconds of mission photography caught six vapour trails.

He landed at Kadena at 0603 GMT, 3 hours 44 minutes after take-off, and the mission was graded a success. The ground crew then found a single hole, "approximately the size which would have been made by a 30.06 shell", in a fillet just aft of the right main landing gear. Whatever made it had passed through the skin and two metal supports, one of them for a fuel tank, and stopped in the structure around the number five tank. It went to Washington by courier, and the analysts judged it debris from a missile, not part of a warhead.

The CIA's analysts later counted at least seven and possibly ten missiles launched during the mission, six to nine of them on the second pass. They suspected the North Vietnamese had moved missile battalions into the Hanoi area to mass fire on a route the A-12s had flown before, and had tried to spoof or saturate the jammers. Even so, they judged the SA-2's chance against an A-12 with its jammers working to be "essentially zero". Kadena saw it differently: one officer reported the pilots "showing considerable anxiety about overflying this area", and Richard Helms suspended the missions. None flew until 8 December, and that one went to the Cambodia-Laos border area; flights over North Vietnam resumed on 15 December, the first two on different routes.

It was the only time enemy fire damaged an A-12. One more missile was fired at an A-12, on 4 January 1968, and burst well over a mile away. Article 129 itself was lost with Jack Weeks over the Pacific in June 1968. The fragments outlived it: in 2013 the CIA announced that it had acquired them, together with the damaged section of the aircraft, a hole torn through its centre, for display in its museum.

differ.text: The records do not agree on the details. The 6 November 1967 memo describes a single hole made by one "pellet"; McIninch and the 27 November analysis call it one piece of debris that was not a warhead pellet; the CIA's 2013 museum story speaks of two small pieces of metal and shows two fragments. Archangel and McIninch say at least six missiles were fired, while the 27 November analysis counts at least seven and possibly ten over the whole mission. The 2013 story says flights over North Vietnam stopped for two months; Archangel's dates (no mission until 8 December, none over the North until 15 December) make it about six weeks.

title: Titanium from the enemy?
dek: The spy plane built to overfly the Soviet Union was supposedly made of Soviet metal bought through front companies; the CIA's own files from the time tell a plainer story.

verdict.text: Unproven, and unlikely for the A-12. The CIA's records from 1960 and 1961 name Titanium Metals Corporation as the supplier and describe a problem of quality, not of quantity. The United States had spare sponge capacity and large government stockpiles, while the Soviet Union was itself trying to buy titanium abroad. In the sources checked, the Soviet-metal story first appears in Ben Rich's memoir of 1994, three decades after the purchases; the CIA's 2007 history repeats it on Rich's word alone, and later versions add details, such as rutile ore and front companies for pizza ovens, that no document supports. Soviet sponge was sold in the West from the mid-1960s, so a purchase for later SR-71 production cannot be ruled out, but no record of one has been found. Say that Rich claimed it; never say that much, or all, of the Blackbirds' titanium was Soviet.

body.text: One of the best Blackbird stories holds that the aircraft built to spy on the Soviet Union was made of Soviet metal. Ben Rich, Lockheed's lead propulsion engineer on the A-12, put it in print in 1994 in a memoir written with Leo Janos. He wrote that the supplier, Titanium Metals Corporation, had "only limited reserves of the precious alloy", so the CIA searched the world and, "using third parties and dummy companies", bought the base metal from one of the world's leading exporters, the Soviet Union, without the Russians ever suspecting what it was for.

Titanium was the only practical answer to the heat. Most of the A-12's skin would run at 500 to 600 F, so Lockheed built over 90 percent of the airframe from a titanium alloy nearly as strong as stainless steel at half the weight; across the Blackbird family titanium alloys made up 93 percent of the structural weight, and Lockheed made more than 13 million titanium parts over 20 years. The early trouble was quality. The CIA's first in-house history (1970-71) records that some 80 percent of the early deliveries from Titanium Metals Corporation had to be rejected, and that supply became consistently satisfactory only in 1961, after a delegation from headquarters visited the company to explain the program's priority.

The agency's files from those years are about quality and secrecy, not Moscow. On 13 January 1960 John Parangosky, deputy chief of the CIA's Development Branch, sent the project's cover officer a trade-press item putting 1959 titanium mill shipments at 3,100 tons, and asked whether Lockheed's planned titanium purchases raised "any cover problems", since production seemed to be closely watched. On 19 April 1961 CIA officers met an official of Titanium Metals Corporation about late deliveries. Their record blames strict quality control and high rejection rates, the time the company needed to learn to process titanium to OXCART specifications, and processing that shuttled metal between its plants. The company promised to fill every outstanding Lockheed order by 1 August 1961, and the memo notes that it was the only supplier Lockheed had found capable of the most complex titanium work.

Kelly Johnson told the same story in 1981. He wrote of working with "our supplier, Titanium Metals Corporation" when the first heat-treated parts came out so brittle that a piece knocked off a desk shattered on the floor, a problem cured by rebuilding Lockheed's acid-pickling line as a copy of the one at the company's mills. His only mention of the USSR in that section is that it had more and larger forging presses than America. Rich's sentence begins with Johnson's words, then goes where Johnson never did. The CIA's 1992 history of the U-2 and OXCART programs, written from the agency's records, also names Titanium Metals Corporation and says nothing of Soviet metal; nor does NASA historian Peter Merlin's 2009 paper.

National figures leave little room for a shortage of raw metal. In 1961, the Bureau of Mines reported, three American firms, among them Titanium Metals Corporation at Henderson, Nevada, produced 6,700 tons of titanium sponge; imports of 2,490 tons came almost entirely from Japan, with small lots from Canada and Britain; and government stockpiles held another 31,007 tons of sponge. Australia produced 88 percent of the world's rutile. A CIA economic study of 1964 found that American sponge capacity had reached about 25,000 metric tons a year, while output had fallen below 4,000 tons in 1959 after bomber cancellations. A Soviet journal admitted in 1962 that production "still lagged behind requirements", and in April 1961 Moscow had made its first approach to buy Japanese titanium, having planned to buy from Britain.

Soviet titanium did reach Western buyers later. CIA analysts reported in 1985 that Soviet exports of sponge and scrap grew from several hundred tons a year in the mid-1960s to a peak of 7,700 tons in 1974, with the United States and West Germany the leading customers. The CIA's own history of the A-12, David Robarge's Archangel (2007, revised 2012), adopted Rich's version, saying some of the scarce base metal "had to be obtained covertly" from the Soviet Union, with Rich's memoir as its only citation. A 2023 National Interest article quotes former SR-71 pilot Col. Richard Graham as saying that America lacked rutile ore and got it from the USSR by "working through Third World countries and bogus operations", one of them, it reports him saying, a front for pizza ovens.

differ.text: Sources disagree on the early rejection rate: Archangel gives 95 percent, in a sentence footnoted to Rich, while McIninch says some 80 percent and Pedlow and Welzenbach up to 80 percent. They also disagree on what was supposedly bought. Rich says base metal from one of the world's leading exporters; Robarge turns this into the country with "the largest known reserves"; Graham, as quoted in 2023, says rutile ore, although Australia then produced 88 percent of the world's rutile and, by the CIA's account, the Soviet industry chose its own low-grade ilmenite over foreign rutile. Claims that Soviet titanium output dwarfed America's are true of the 1980s (the CIA estimated about 71,000 metric tons in 1984, more than five times US output) but not of the A-12 years, when it estimated that the USSR turned about 5,000 metric tons of sponge into mill products in 1963 against American sponge production of 7,200 tons.

title: Thrown clear at Mach 3.18
dek: Bill Weaver never pulled his ejection handle. His SR-71 came apart around him at 78,000 feet, and he woke up falling.

body.text: On 25 January 1966 SR-71A 61-7952 took off from Edwards Air Force Base on a Lockheed test flight. Bill Weaver, a Lockheed test pilot, was in the front seat; behind him was Jim Zwayer, a Lockheed flight test specialist in reconnaissance and navigation systems. They were to evaluate those systems and to try flying with the centre of gravity further aft than normal, which cut trim drag at high Mach but made the aircraft less stable in pitch.

Weaver's own account describes what happened after they refuelled and turned east. At Mach 3.2 and 78,000 ft the right inlet's automatic control failed and he switched it to manual. In a planned 35-degree bank to the right the right inlet unstarted; the aircraft rolled further right and pitched up, and full left and forward stick did nothing. He wrote that he did not think an ejection at Mach 3.18 and 78,800 ft was survivable, and tried to tell Zwayer to stay with the aircraft, but the g-forces garbled his words.

He later learned that only two or three seconds passed between the unstart and the loss of control. He blacked out, and the SR-71 disintegrated around him. A reconstruction published by The X-Hunters, an aviation archaeology group, says the airframe failed at the main joint just ahead of the wings. The CIA's accident summary records that the pilot was "forcibly ripped from seat through lap belt and shoulder harness by wind and pressure forces" as the aircraft broke up.

Weaver wrote that he came to thinking he was dreaming, then that he must be dead, and that being dead did not seem so bad. He was falling, blind behind an iced-over face plate, his pressure suit inflated by the emergency oxygen in his seat kit. He was falling steadily rather than tumbling, so he reasoned that the small stabilising parachute had opened, and as he groped for the D-ring his main parachute opened by itself. Holding up the face plate, whose latch had broken, he saw a second parachute about a quarter of a mile away.

He landed in northeastern New Mexico, about 1.5 miles from the ranch house of Albert Mitchell Jr., who had watched the parachutes come down and flew out in his helicopter. Weaver found his lap belt and shoulder harness, shredded but still latched, hanging around him: his ejection seat had never left the aircraft. Mitchell flew to the other parachute and came back with the news that Zwayer was dead, apparently from a broken neck suffered in the break-up, then flew Weaver about 60 miles to the hospital at Tucumcari.

citations.detail: passage beginning "The citizens of Buyeros and Albert"

body.text: The CIA's accident summary, prepared on 11 January 1967, puts the crash 107 nautical miles from Cannon Air Force Base on a bearing of 350 degrees, with wreckage strewn over an area about 16 miles long and 5 miles wide, and gives the primary cause as fuel distribution that left an unsafe centre of gravity. The accident board asked for the sharp edges on lap belt adjusters to be removed, for face plate heating during free fall and for a study of automatic ejection in a high-altitude break-up. Weaver wrote that the flight was repeated in the SR-71 simulator at Beale the next day with the same outcome, and that testing with an aft centre of gravity was stopped.
Two weeks later Weaver was back in an SR-71, flying the first sortie of a new aircraft at Palmdale. Zwayer remains the only person killed in an SR-71.

differ.text: Weaver gives Mach 3.18 and 78,800 ft at the moment of the unstart; The X-Hunters give Mach 3.17 and nearly 78,000 ft. The CIA summary puts the debris over about 16 by 5 miles, while Weaver and The X-Hunters say 15 by 10 miles. The CIA summary records Zwayer's death as a "fatal ejection" and says the manner in which his seat was fired is unknown, whereas Weaver wrote that both men were ripped out of the airplane. The summary names an unsafe centre of gravity as the primary cause; Weaver describes the cumulative effect of the inlet malfunction, reduced stability, the turn and the speed.

title: New York to the Suez Canal and back
dek: In October 1973 the White House wanted to see the war for itself, and the SR-71 it sent flew there and back from New York in eleven hours, refuelling six times on the way.

body.text: On the morning of 9 October 1973, three days after Egyptian and Syrian forces attacked Israeli positions in Sinai and on the Golan Heights, Henry Kissinger held a principals-only meeting of the Washington Special Actions Group in the White House Situation Room, with Defense Secretary James Schlesinger, Deputy Secretary of State Kenneth Rush, Admiral Thomas Moorer of the Joint Chiefs and William Colby of the CIA. Israel had called all night for supplies. When Schlesinger said they needed to know about the bridges, Kissinger answered, in the words of the meeting record: "We should fly the SR-71." Before the group broke up, Moorer asked whether the paperwork could be done.

On 11 October the Joint Chiefs ordered Strategic Air Command to send SR-71s to Griffiss Air Force Base, New York, and two SR-71As of the 9th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing came from Beale, California. A Middle East plan, GIANT REACH, already existed: the SR-71 would take off from Beale and land after the mission at a base whose name, like the reason it could not be used, is still blacked out in the declassified SAC chronology. Either way, SAC had to plan round trips from the United States, which doubled the tanker force. Two CIA U-2s, deployed on 7 and 8 October to be ready to cover the war, were never tasked.

The first sortie left Griffiss at 0600 GMT on 13 October, flown by Lt. Col. James Shelton with Lt. Col. Gary Coleman as reconnaissance systems officer. Reaching the targets took three air refuellings, over the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, at a point still withheld and south of Crete; three more, south of Crete, off Portugal and over the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, brought the aircraft back to Griffiss at 1713 GMT. The flight lasted 11 hours 13 minutes, beating the SR-71's endurance record of 10 hours 30 minutes from April 1971, and needed 14 KC-135Q tankers. Shelton described the mission and its six refuellings in a talk at the Western Museum of Flight, posted in 2016.

On 16 October Colby brought prints to the Situation Room. "They flew right down the Canal," he said. Taken on Saturday 13 October, they showed the Egyptians across the canal to about 8 km, as the Israelis had claimed, and nothing to support claims of huge tank losses, though Moorer warned that a shell through an engine would not show. But when Colby asked about the next flight, Kissinger demurred: the Egyptians, he said, had "been very restrained about it". The meeting put the second mission on hold.

citations.detail: Document 191, summary of conclusions and pp. 546 to 552, with footnote 4

body.text: Colby wanted another flight "around ceasefire time" as a baseline, and on 24 October the group agreed one should run down the canal and over Egypt; Kissinger asked only whether it could avoid Cairo. At lunch he remarked that if anyone complained about the next day's flight, Washington could say it was "to fix the ceasefire lines". On 25 October Capt. Eldon Joersz and Capt. John Fuller flew it, refuelling south of Nova Scotia, north of the Azores and south of Crete, and launched and landed at the same times as the first crew. On 31 October Moorer, citing evidence of Scud missiles in Egypt, asked for a third; after an overcast delay, on 4 November Capt. Robert Helt and Capt. Larry Elliott flew 11 hours 22 minutes, the longest SR-71 flight yet.

citations.detail: pp. 2 to 3 (PDF pp. 3 to 4), entries for 25 October and 4 November

body.text: The round trips were costly: on 6 November Vice Admiral John Weinel, for the Joint Chiefs, put a flight from New York at about half a million dollars, against $175,000 to $200,000 from Europe; on 29 November Moorer added that each used 230,000 gallons of fuel. With fuel due to reach RAF Mildenhall in England on 1 January, the group agreed on one more flight from the United States and later ones from Britain. By then, according to a veterans' timeline published by Roadrunners Internationale, GIANT REACH had moved on 15 November to Seymour Johnson Air Force Base, North Carolina.

body.text: The flights outlasted the fighting. Under the Egyptian-Israeli disengagement of January 1974, the United States told both governments it would photograph the disengagement areas about every ten days to two weeks and give each side the pictures. When Colby asked on 22 January whether the U-2 would do, Kissinger replied: "I told them SR-71." The Roadrunners timeline counts nine GIANT REACH sorties, the last on 6 April 1974. The CIA was then tasked to watch the disengagement areas with U-2s, and its detachment reached its still-redacted base on 21 April.

differ.text: The SAC chronology dates the first sortie 13 October, and the editors of Foreign Relations date the photographs shown on 16 October to the same day, but on 1 November Kissinger told Golda Meir that the SR-71 had photographed only twice, on the 12th and the 25th. Written on 12 December 1973, the chronology records three sorties (13 and 25 October, 4 November). On 29 November Moorer told the group that the last flight had been on 18 November, whereas the Roadrunners timeline, which credits its entries to SR-71 veteran Buddy Brown, lists a sortie on 11 November and none on 18 November, and counts nine in all to April 1974. The airframe serials (61-7979 for the first three sorties, 61-7964 on 11 November and 2 December) come only from that timeline. The chronology spells the third RSO's name Elliot.
